questions.prompt: An `Invoice` class has `CalculateTotal()`, `SaveToDatabase()` and `PrintInvoice()`. Which principle does it break?
options: Single Responsibility: it has three reasons to change
Liskov Substitution: it can't replace its base class
Interface Segregation: its interface is too small
Dependency Inversion: it depends on an abstraction
questions.explanation: A class should have only one reason to change. Calculating, saving and printing are three jobs, so the fix splits them into `InvoiceCalculator`, `InvoiceRepository` and `InvoicePrinter`.

questions.prompt: `DiscountCalculator.GetDiscount` uses `if (customerType == "Regular")` and `if (customerType == "Premium")`. A new "Gold" type arrives. How does the lesson's Open/Closed fix handle it?
options: Add another `if` branch to `GetDiscount`
Add a `GoldDiscount : IDiscountStrategy` class without changing `DiscountCalculator`
Make `GetDiscount` throw for unknown types
Move the `if` chain into a static helper class
questions.explanation: Open for extension, closed for modification: `DiscountCalculator.Calculate` takes an `IDiscountStrategy`, so new discount types are new classes and existing code stays untouched.

questions.prompt: What happens when `MakeBirdFly` is called with an `Ostrich`?
options: It prints `Flying!`, because `MakeBirdFly` takes a `Bird`
It throws `NotSupportedException` with the message "Ostriches can't fly!"
It fails to compile, because `Ostrich` can't override `Fly`
It prints nothing and returns normally
questions.explanation: The override runs and throws. That breaks Liskov Substitution: code written for any `Bird` can't safely receive an `Ostrich`. The fix moves flying into a separate `IFlyable` interface.

questions.prompt: `Robot` implements `IWorker` and has to write `Eat() { throw new NotImplementedException(); }`. What is the lesson's fix?
options: Make `Eat()` virtual so `Robot` can skip it
Have `Robot` inherit from `Human` instead
Split the interface into `IWorkable` and `IEatable`, and have `Robot` implement only `IWorkable`
Catch the exception wherever `Eat()` is called
questions.explanation: Interface Segregation says a class should not be forced to implement methods it doesn't use, so the interface is split into small, focused ones.

questions.prompt: `NotificationManager` creates `new EmailService()` in a field. What does Dependency Inversion change?
options: It makes `EmailService` a static class
It makes `NotificationManager` inherit from `EmailService`
It moves `Send` into `NotificationManager`
It injects an `IMessageSender` through the constructor, so email, SMS or a future sender can be used
questions.explanation: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. Taking `IMessageSender` in the constructor removes the tight coupling to `EmailService`.
